beats.narration: Begin by framing Introduction to Thesis Preparation as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Students work with a supervising faculty member to complete their undergraduate thesis proposal, and do additional background preparation (for example, programming, study, exercises, and analysis) for the subject area and specific problem(s) to be addressed in a thesis. Consider this worked case: A student collaborates with their advisor to draft a proposal that outlines a machine learning project on educational data analysis. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Introduction to Thesis Preparation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a simple flowchart showing the sequence: Advisor Consultation -> Background Preparation -> Proposal Drafting -> Advisor Review.

beats.narration: Now define Defining the Research Problem precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience. Consider this worked case: Students transform a broad interest in 'AI ethics' into a focused question about 'bias detection in automated grading tools. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Defining the Research Problem
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a Venn diagram comparing broad interests, literature gaps, and a clearly defined research question.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Methodology and Reproducibility operates in a concrete sequence. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Consider this worked case: Students document exact software versions, dataset sources, and step-by-step procedures for their thesis experiment. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Methodology and Reproducibility
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a checklist template with fields for 'Dataset Source', 'Code Repository', 'Parameter Settings', and 'Reproduction Steps'.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Ethical Computing Standards and make the decision criteria explicit. Computing professionals should avoid harm. Consider this worked case: Students include a section in their proposal detailing how they will anonymize student data and obtain necessary permissions. 'Potential Harm' with checkmarks for privacy, fairness, and transparency. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Ethical Computing Standards
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a side-by-side comparison of 'Ethical Compliance' vs. 'Potential Harm' with checkmarks for privacy, fairness, and transparency.

beats.narration: Apply Responsible Technical Communication to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. Consider this worked case: Students structure their proposal to clearly separate their novel hypothesis from established literature findings. 'Evidence' (prior research citations), with arrows linking them. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Responsible Technical Communication
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a two-column layout: 'Claim' (student's contribution) vs. 'Evidence' (prior research citations), with arrows linking them.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Results and Limitations, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Consider this worked case: Students draft a subsection explicitly stating potential biases in their dataset and how they will validate their findings. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Results and Limitations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a template box labeled 'Limitations & Threats to Validity' with prompts for data constraints, methodological gaps, and mitigation strategies.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Research Integrity and Plagiarism with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Consider this worked case: Students use citation management tools to track all references and verify that all code and data are properly attributed. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Plagiarism
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a flowchart: 'Source Identification' -> 'Citation Formatting' -> 'Plagiarism Check' -> 'Integrity Verification'.

beats.narration: Use Supervisor Deliverables and Planning to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Additional deliverables set by the advisor are also required (for example, source code, bibliographies, notes, presentations, etc. Consider this worked case: Students create a project management tracker that logs weekly milestones for coding, literature review, and draft presentations. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Supervisor Deliverables and Planning
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a Gantt chart template with phases: 'Proposal Draft', 'Code Setup', 'Literature Review', 'Advisor Feedback', 'Final Submission'.

beats.narration: Connect Evaluation Criteria and Quality Standards to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. Consider this worked case: Students apply a rubric that scores their proposal on clarity, methodological rigor, ethical compliance, and alignment with advisor goals. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Evaluation Criteria and Quality Standards
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a scoring matrix with categories: 'Problem Definition', 'Methodology', 'Ethics', 'Communication', and 'Feasibility' with 1-5 scales.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. At the end of the semester, a thesis proposal must be submitted for approval to the advisor. Consider this worked case: Students run a final review against a checklist: problem statement, literature review, reproducible methods, ethical considerations, citations, and advisor deliverables. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a printable checklist template with checkboxes for each requirement, a signature line for advisor approval, and a submission deadline field.

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.
sources.title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.
